decks.title: Recurring deposits — Part 1: How the interest is earned
goals: Explain how a recurring deposit account works
Find the principal for one month from the monthly balances
Calculate the interest with the formula, with the period in months
Explain why the interest grows faster than the period

slides.heading: Banking: Recurring Deposit Accounts, Part 1
slides.body_md: Save a fixed sum every month; the bank adds interest. How much interest?

nodes.label: The balance grows by $P$ each month
Each instalment earns simple interest for its own months

visual.alt: Flow chart of a recurring deposit: pay a fixed sum every month, the balance grows by one instalment each month, each instalment earns simple interest for the months it stays, and at maturity the bank pays the instalments plus the interest.
visual.caption: How a recurring deposit works.

slides.narration: Welcome to recurring deposits. Many families save by paying a fixed amount into the bank every month, for a year, two years or more. At the end, the bank returns all the instalments with interest. In this part we find out exactly how that interest is worked out, and why it is less than you might first think.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Find the **principal for one month** from the monthly balances
Use the interest formula with $n$ in **months**
slides.narration: These are your goals for part one. We start with how the account works, then build the interest formula from a simple table of monthly balances. Once you understand where the formula comes from, you will not forget it, and you will avoid the most common mistakes.

slides.heading: What is a recurring deposit?
slides.body_md: A **recurring deposit** account collects a fixed **monthly instalment** $P$ for $n$ months. The bank pays simple interest at $r\%$ per annum and returns everything at **maturity**.

rows: the fixed sum paid every month
simple interest earned on all the instalments
amount paid back at the end

visual.alt: Table of recurring-deposit terms: monthly instalment P, period n in months, rate r per cent per annum, interest I and maturity value MV.
visual.caption: The language of recurring deposits.

slides.narration: In a recurring deposit, you choose a monthly instalment and a period, say twelve or twenty four months. You pay the same amount every month. The bank quotes a rate of interest per year. At the end of the period, called maturity, you get back all your instalments plus the interest. Learn the letters: P, n, r and I.

slides.heading: Each instalment stays a different time
slides.body_md: For ₹$500$ a month for $6$ months, the first instalment is in the bank for all $6$ months, the last for only $1$.

visual.alt: Table for an instalment of 500 rupees for 6 months at 8 per cent: the first instalment earns interest for 6 months, the second for 5, down to 1 month for the sixth; the interests add up to 70 rupees.
visual.caption: The first instalment earns for $6$ months, the last for only $1$.

slides.narration: Here is the key idea. The first instalment is paid in month one and stays for all six months. The second stays five months, and so on, down to the last, which stays just one month. So the money is not all in the bank for the whole period. Each instalment earns simple interest only for its own time.

slides.heading: Monthly balances: the principal for one month
slides.body_md: Add the balance at the end of every month. This sum earns interest for **one month**:

visual.alt: Table of monthly balances for 500 rupees a month: 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500 and 3000 rupees; their sum, 10500 rupees, is the principal for one month.
visual.caption: Sum of balances $= 500 \times 21 = 10500$.

slides.narration: Another way to see it: look at the balance at the end of each month. It grows by one instalment every month. If we add up all these balances, we get a single sum that earns interest for just one month. For five hundred rupees over six months, the balances add up to ten thousand five hundred rupees.

slides.heading: The interest formula
slides.body_md: Simple interest on the principal for one month, for $\dfrac{1}{12}$ of a year, at $r\%$:

visual.alt: Flow showing how the interest formula is built: the sum of the monthly balances, P times n times n plus 1 over 2, earns interest for one month, one twelfth of a year, at r per cent.
visual.caption: Simple interest on the principal for one month.

slides.narration: Now we build the formula. The principal for one month is P times n times n plus one, over two. One month is one twelfth of a year. So we multiply by one twelfth, and by r over one hundred. That gives the interest formula used by the board. Remember that n is the number of months and r is the rate per year.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a six-month deposit
slides.body_md: Find the interest on ₹$500$ a month for $6$ months at $8\%$ per annum.

visual.alt: Working table for 500 rupees a month for 6 months at 8 per cent: n times n plus 1 over 2 is 21, the principal for one month is 10500 rupees and the interest is 70 rupees.
visual.caption: Interest ₹$70$.

slides.narration: Write P, n and r first. The principal for one month is five hundred times twenty one, which is ten thousand five hundred rupees. One twelfth of a year at eight per cent gives seventy rupees. The full formula gives the same answer in one line. Notice how small the interest is compared with the three thousand rupees deposited.

slides.heading: Quick check: the principal for one month
slides.body_md: Add the balances, or use $P \times \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$.
slides.narration: Find n times n plus one, halve it, and multiply by the monthly instalment.

slides.heading: Changing the period into months
slides.body_md: The rate is per **annum** but $n$ is always in **months**. Useful values:

visual.alt: Table of periods and their values of n and n times n plus 1 over 2: 6 months gives 21, one year 78, one and a half years 171, two years 300, two and a half years 465 and three years 666.
visual.caption: Change years to months first.

slides.narration: Before using the formula, always change the period into months. One and a half years is eighteen months, two years is twenty four, three years is thirty six. This table gives the value of n times n plus one over two for common periods. You will meet seventy eight, three hundred and six hundred and sixty six again and again.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: one and a half years
slides.body_md: Ira pays ₹$800$ a month for $1.5$ years at $7\%$ per annum. Find the interest.

visual.alt: Working table for 800 rupees a month for 18 months at 7 per cent: n times n plus 1 over 2 is 171, the principal for one month is 136800 rupees and the interest is 798 rupees.
visual.caption: Interest ₹$798$.

slides.narration: First, one and a half years becomes eighteen months. Then eighteen times nineteen over two is one hundred and seventy one. Multiply by eight hundred rupees for the principal for one month. Finally, take one twelfth of a year at seven per cent. Ira earns seven hundred and ninety eight rupees.

slides.heading: Quick check: a two-year value
slides.body_md: Change the period into months first.
slides.narration: Two years is how many months? Multiply that by the next whole number, then halve.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a rate with a decimal
slides.body_md: Find the interest on ₹$1250$ a month for $2$ years at $6.5\%$ per annum.
bullets: **Tip —** Keep the paise; do not round until the last step.

visual.alt: Working table for 1250 rupees a month for 24 months at 6.5 per cent: n times n plus 1 over 24 is 25, and the interest is 2031.25 rupees.
visual.caption: Paise matter: ₹2,031.25.

slides.narration: Two years is twenty four months. A neat shortcut: twenty four times twenty five over twenty four is just twenty five. So the interest is twelve hundred and fifty, times twenty five, times six point five over one hundred. The answer has paise: two thousand and thirty one rupees and twenty five paise. Keep them.

slides.heading: Interest grows faster than the period
slides.body_md: For ₹$1000$ a month at $6\%$: $12$ months give ₹$390$, but $24$ months give ₹$1500$, almost four times as much.

functions.label: if interest were proportional to n

visual.alt: Graph of the interest on a recurring deposit of 1000 rupees a month at 6 per cent against the number of months: a curve rising faster and faster through 390 at 12 months, 1500 at 24 months and 3330 at 36 months, above a straight line that would give only 780 at 24 months.
visual.caption: Doubling the period from $12$ to $24$ months multiplies the interest by almost $4$.

slides.narration: Look at the graph. If interest grew in proportion to the months, it would follow the straight line, and doubling the period would double the interest. But the curve bends upwards. With a longer deposit, there are more instalments, and the early ones stay longer. Twelve months earn three hundred and ninety rupees; twenty four months earn fifteen hundred.

slides.heading: Quick check: doubling the period
slides.body_md: Does the interest double when the period doubles?
slides.narration: Think about the graph. Compare n times n plus one for twelve and for twenty four months.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: same deposits, different interest
slides.body_md: At $8\%$ per annum, Ritu pays ₹$600$ a month for $24$ months and Kabir ₹$1200$ a month for $12$ months. Both deposit ₹14,400. Who earns more interest?
bullets: **Answer —** Ritu earns ₹$576$ more, because her money stays in the bank longer on average.

visual.alt: Comparison table: Ritu pays 600 rupees for 24 months and Kabir 1200 rupees for 12 months, both depositing 14400 rupees at 8 per cent; Ritu earns 1200 rupees of interest and Kabir 624 rupees.
visual.caption: Same deposits, very different interest.

slides.narration: Both friends deposit fourteen thousand four hundred rupees. Ritu spreads it over twenty four months and earns twelve hundred rupees. Kabir pays it in twelve months and earns only six hundred and twenty four. The difference is five hundred and seventy six rupees. The longer deposit wins, because its early instalments stay much longer.

slides.heading: Quick check: ratio of interests
slides.body_md: Compare $n(n+1)$ for the two periods.
slides.narration: With the same instalment and rate, the interest depends only on n times n plus one. Work out both values and simplify the ratio.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: A recurring deposit: fixed instalment $P$ every month for $n$ months

visual.alt: Summary table: the principal for one month is P times n times n plus 1 over 2; the interest formula; n is in months and r per annum; interest grows like n times n plus 1.
visual.caption: Part 1 in four lines.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. A recurring deposit collects equal monthly instalments. Each instalment earns simple interest only for the months it stays. Adding the monthly balances gives the principal for one month, and this leads to the interest formula. Always use n in months and r per year.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Interest (3 marks):** $n$ in months 1 + substitution in the formula 1 + answer 1
**Mistake:** simple interest on the whole deposit for the whole period
slides.narration: In the exam, write the formula first, then substitute with n in months. That line earns a mark even if the arithmetic slips. Watch out for three traps: using years for n, forgetting the two in the denominator, and charging interest on all the money for the whole period. Keep paise until the end.

decks.title: Recurring deposits — Part 2: Maturity value and inverse problems
goals: Calculate the maturity value of a recurring deposit
Find the monthly instalment from the maturity value or the interest
Find the number of months by solving a quadratic equation

slides.heading: Banking: Recurring Deposit Accounts, Part 2
slides.body_md: What do you get back, and how do you plan for a target amount?

visual.alt: Graph of the maturity value of a recurring deposit of 1000 rupees a month at 6 per cent against the number of months: 12390 rupees at 12 months, 25500 at 24 and 39330 at 36, above the straight line of the total deposited, 36000 at 36 months; the gap is the interest.
visual.caption: The gap between the curve and the line is the interest.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. At maturity the bank returns your instalments plus the interest. That total is the maturity value. We will calculate it, and then turn the question around: if you know what you want at the end, what instalment, rate or period do you need? These are the inverse problems the board loves to ask.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Find the **number of months** from a quadratic
Check every answer by working forwards
slides.narration: These are your goals for part two. The first is direct. The next three are inverse problems. Finding the instalment or the rate needs only a linear equation. Finding the number of months needs a quadratic equation, and you must choose the right root.

slides.heading: Maturity value
slides.body_md: At maturity the bank pays back every instalment and the interest:

visual.alt: Flow showing the maturity value as the total deposited, P times n, plus the interest I.
visual.caption: What the bank pays at the end.

slides.narration: The maturity value is simply the total you deposited, P times n, plus the interest I. So always find the interest first, using the formula from part one, and then add the deposits. Read the question carefully: sometimes it asks only for the interest, sometimes for the amount received at maturity.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a three-year deposit
slides.body_md: Find the maturity value of ₹$1500$ a month for $3$ years at $7.5\%$ per annum.

visual.alt: Working table for 1500 rupees a month for 3 years at 7.5 per cent: n is 36, the deposits are 54000 rupees, the interest is 6243.75 rupees and the maturity value is 60243.75 rupees.
visual.caption: Maturity value ₹60,243.75.

slides.narration: Three years is thirty six months, so the deposits total fifty four thousand rupees. The interest formula gives six thousand two hundred and forty three rupees and seventy five paise. Add the two to get the maturity value, sixty thousand two hundred and forty three rupees and seventy five paise.

slides.heading: Deposits and maturity value side by side
slides.body_md: For ₹$1000$ a month at $6\%$, the deposits grow evenly but the interest grows faster.

visual.alt: Table for 1000 rupees a month at 6 per cent: after 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 and 36 months the interest is 105, 390, 855, 1500, 2325 and 3330 rupees, added to the deposits to give the maturity value.
visual.caption: Deposits grow evenly; interest grows faster.

slides.narration: This table follows one deposit of a thousand rupees a month. Every six months, the deposits rise by six thousand rupees. The interest, though, rises faster each time: one hundred and five, then three hundred and ninety, then eight hundred and fifty five, and so on. Their sum is the maturity value.

slides.heading: Quick check: a maturity value
slides.body_md: Interest first, then add the deposits.
slides.narration: Write n, find the interest with the formula, then add P times n.

slides.heading: Inverse problems: what is unknown?
slides.body_md: The same two formulas can be read backwards. Decide which quantity is unknown:

visual.alt: Decision chart for inverse problems: if the instalment or the rate is unknown, the equation is linear; if the number of months is unknown, the equation is quadratic; always check by working forwards.
visual.caption: Three kinds of inverse problem.

slides.narration: In an inverse problem, the maturity value or the interest is given and something else is unknown. If the instalment or the rate is unknown, it appears only once, so the equation is linear. If the number of months is unknown, it appears as n and as n times n plus one, so the equation is quadratic.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: finding the instalment
slides.body_md: A $2$-year deposit at $9\%$ per annum matures to ₹31,500. Find the monthly instalment.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Let the monthly instalment be ₹$P$. Then $I = P \times \dfrac{24 \times 25}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{9}{100} = 2.25P$.

visual.alt: Steps for finding the instalment: interest 2.25 P, maturity value 26.25 P, equation 26.25 P equals 31500, so P is 1200 rupees.
visual.caption: Everything is a multiple of $P$.

slides.narration: Let the instalment be P. The interest is P times three hundred over twelve times nine over one hundred, which is two point two five P. The deposits are twenty four P. So the maturity value is twenty six point two five P. Divide thirty one thousand five hundred by twenty six point two five: the instalment is twelve hundred rupees.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: finding the rate
slides.body_md: Zoya pays ₹$2000$ a month for $15$ months and receives ₹31,600. Find the rate.

visual.alt: Steps for finding the rate: deposits 30000 rupees, interest 1600 rupees, interest in terms of r is 200 r, so r is 8 per cent.
visual.caption: Find the interest first.

slides.narration: First take away the deposits: thirty thousand rupees. The interest is sixteen hundred rupees. Now write the interest formula with r unknown. Fifteen times sixteen over twenty four is ten, so the interest is two hundred r. Two hundred r equals sixteen hundred, so the rate is eight per cent per year.

slides.heading: Quick check: find the rate
slides.body_md: Write the interest as a multiple of $r$.
slides.narration: Work out the interest on the deposit for a rate of one per cent. How many of those make the given interest?

slides.heading: Finding the number of months
slides.body_md: With $n$ unknown, the maturity value gives a **quadratic** in $n$:

visual.alt: Steps for finding the number of months: 18960 equals 1200 n plus 4 n times n plus 1; in standard form n squared plus 301 n minus 4740 equals zero; factorising gives n equals 15 or minus 316, and the negative root is rejected.
visual.caption: Reject the negative root.

slides.narration: When the period is unknown, n appears twice: in the deposits, P times n, and in the interest, through n times n plus one. Expanding gives a quadratic equation. Make the coefficient of n squared equal to one, then factorise or use the quadratic formula. One root is always negative, and we reject it.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: months from the maturity value
slides.body_md: A deposit of ₹$1200$ a month at $8\%$ per annum matures to ₹18,960. For how many months?
bullets: **Step 4 —** $(n - 15)(n + 316) = 0$, so $n = 15$ or $n = -316$. The number of months cannot be negative, so $n = 15$.

visual.alt: Steps for finding the number of months: 18960 equals 1200 n plus 4 n times n plus 1; in standard form n squared plus 301 n minus 4740 equals zero; factorising gives n equals 15 or minus 316, and the negative root is rejected.
visual.caption: Reject the negative root.

slides.narration: Here P times r over twenty four hundred is four, so the interest is four n times n plus one. The equation becomes four n squared plus twelve hundred and four n minus eighteen thousand nine hundred and sixty equals zero. Divide by four and factorise. The roots are fifteen and minus three hundred and sixteen, so the deposit ran for fifteen months.

slides.heading: Quick check: choose the root
slides.body_md: Factorise, then keep the sensible root.
slides.narration: Find two numbers that multiply to minus four hundred and twenty and add to one. Which root can be a number of months?

slides.heading: Worked example 5: months from the interest
slides.body_md: A deposit of ₹$500$ a month at $10\%$ per annum earns ₹$1150$ as interest. Find the number of months.

visual.alt: Steps for finding the months from the interest: n times n plus 1 equals 552, so n squared plus n minus 552 equals zero, which factorises to give n equals 23.
visual.caption: Two consecutive numbers whose product is $552$: $23 \times 24$.

slides.narration: When only the interest is given, the deposits do not appear, so the equation is simpler. Make n times n plus one the subject: it equals five hundred and fifty two. Look for two consecutive whole numbers with that product: twenty three and twenty four. So the deposit ran for twenty three months.

slides.heading: Quick check: both roots?
slides.body_md: Can a negative root be a period?
slides.narration: Think about what n means in this chapter before deciding.

slides.heading: Always check by working forwards
slides.body_md: Put each answer back into the formulas.

visual.alt: Table checking each inverse answer by working forwards: instalment 1200 gives maturity value 31500, rate 8 gives 31600, 15 months gives 18960, and 23 months gives interest 1150 rupees.
visual.caption: Put your answer back into the formula.

slides.narration: Inverse problems are easy to check. Put your answer back into the interest formula and the maturity value formula, and see whether you get the given amount. Each answer on this slide passes the check. In an exam, one line of checking can save you from losing marks for a slip in the algebra.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Instalment: write MV or $I$ as a multiple of $P$
Rate: $I = \text{MV} - Pn$, then a multiple of $r$
Months: a quadratic in $n$; keep the positive whole-number root

rows: write MV (or $I$) as a multiple of $P$; divide
$I = \text{MV} - Pn$; write $I$ as a multiple of $r$
quadratic in $n$; keep the positive whole-number root

visual.alt: Summary table: the maturity value is P times n plus I; for the instalment write the maturity value as a multiple of P; for the rate find I and write it as a multiple of r; for the months solve a quadratic and keep the positive whole-number root.
visual.caption: Part 2 in four lines.

slides.narration: To sum up part two. The maturity value is the deposits plus the interest. To find the instalment or the rate, write everything as a multiple of the unknown and divide. To find the number of months, solve a quadratic and keep the positive whole-number root. Then check your answer by working forwards.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Maturity value (3 marks):** interest 2 + adding the deposits 1
**Instalment or rate (3–4 marks):** equation 1–2 + solving 1 + answer 1
**Months (4 marks):** equation in $n$ 1 + standard form 1 + factorising 1 + answer with the negative root rejected 1
**Mistake:** forgetting to subtract the deposits before finding the rate
**Mistake:** giving the interest when the maturity value is asked
slides.narration: For a maturity value, most marks are for the interest, so show the formula. For the instalment or rate, write the equation clearly. For the number of months, the steps are: the equation, the standard form, the factorisation and the answer, with a word on why the negative root is rejected. Read whether the question wants the interest or the maturity value.

notes.title: Banking: Recurring Deposit Accounts — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. How a recurring deposit works
sections.body_md:
In a **recurring deposit** (RD) account a depositor pays a fixed **monthly instalment** $P$ for a fixed number of months $n$. The bank pays **simple interest** at $r\%$ **per annum** on each instalment for the time it stays in the account, and returns the instalments with the interest at **maturity**.

- The 1st instalment earns interest for $n$ months, the 2nd for $n - 1$ months, …, the last for $1$ month.
- A recurring deposit suits people who can save a little every month rather than a lump sum.

key_terms.definition_md: A bank account into which a fixed sum is paid every month for a fixed number of months.
The fixed sum $P$ paid every month.
The end of the period, when the bank pays back the instalments with the interest.

nodes.label: The balance grows by $P$ each month
Each instalment earns simple interest for its own months

visual.alt: Flow chart of a recurring deposit: pay a fixed sum every month, the balance grows by one instalment each month, each instalment earns simple interest for the months it stays, and at maturity the bank pays the instalments plus the interest.

sections.heading: 2. Monthly balances and the principal for one month
sections.body_md:
At the end of month $k$ the balance is $kP$. The sum of the balances,

$$P + 2P + \cdots + nP = P \times \frac{n(n+1)}{2},$$

earns simple interest for **one month**. It is called the principal for one month. *Example:* ₹$500$ a month for $6$ months: $500 \times 21 = 10500$.

key_terms.definition_md: The sum of the monthly balances, $P \times \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$, which earns interest for one month.

visual.alt: Table of monthly balances for 500 rupees a month: 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2500 and 3000 rupees; their sum, 10500 rupees, is the principal for one month.
visual.caption: Sum of balances $= 500 \times 21 = 10500$.

visuals.alt: Table for an instalment of 500 rupees for 6 months at 8 per cent: the first instalment earns interest for 6 months, the second for 5, down to 1 month for the sixth; the interests add up to 70 rupees.
visuals.caption: The first instalment earns for $6$ months, the last for only $1$.

sections.heading: 3. The interest formula
sections.body_md:
Simple interest on the principal for one month, for $\dfrac{1}{12}$ of a year at $r\%$:

$$I = P \times \frac{n(n+1)}{2 \times 12} \times \frac{r}{100}.$$

- $n$ is in **months** (1.5 years $= 18$, 2 years $= 24$, 3 years $= 36$); $r$ is per **annum**.
- *Example:* ₹$800$ a month for $18$ months at $7\%$: $I = 800 \times \dfrac{18 \times 19}{24} \times \dfrac{7}{100} = 798$.
- Keep paise: ₹$1250$ for $24$ months at $6.5\%$ gives ₹2,031.25.

key_terms.definition_md: The yearly rate of interest $r\%$; the formula converts one month to $\dfrac{1}{12}$ of a year.

visual.alt: Flow showing how the interest formula is built: the sum of the monthly balances, P times n times n plus 1 over 2, earns interest for one month, one twelfth of a year, at r per cent.
visual.caption: Simple interest on the principal for one month.

visuals.alt: Table of periods and their values of n and n times n plus 1 over 2: 6 months gives 21, one year 78, one and a half years 171, two years 300, two and a half years 465 and three years 666.
visuals.caption: Change years to months first.

sections.heading: 4. How the interest grows
sections.body_md:
With $P$ and $r$ fixed, the interest is proportional to $n(n+1)$, **not** to $n$. Doubling the period from $12$ to $24$ months multiplies $n(n+1)$ from $156$ to $600$: almost four times.

For the same total deposited, a longer deposit with smaller instalments earns more: ₹$600$ for $24$ months earns ₹$1200$ at $8\%$, ₹$1200$ for $12$ months only ₹$624$.

visual.caption: Doubling the period from $12$ to $24$ months multiplies the interest by almost $4$.

sections.heading: 5. Maturity value
sections.body_md:
The maturity value is the total deposited plus the interest:

$$\text{MV} = P \times n + I.$$

*Example:* ₹$1500$ a month for $3$ years at $7.5\%$: deposits $54000$, interest $6243.75$, maturity value ₹60,243.75. If the instalment is doubled (same $n$ and $r$), the maturity value doubles.

key_terms.definition_md: The amount paid at maturity: total of the instalments plus the interest.

visual.alt: Graph of the maturity value of a recurring deposit of 1000 rupees a month at 6 per cent against the number of months: 12390 rupees at 12 months, 25500 at 24 and 39330 at 36, above the straight line of the total deposited, 36000 at 36 months; the gap is the interest.
visual.caption: The gap between the curve and the line is the interest.

visuals.alt: Table for 1000 rupees a month at 6 per cent: after 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 and 36 months the interest is 105, 390, 855, 1500, 2325 and 3330 rupees, added to the deposits to give the maturity value.
visuals.caption: Deposits grow evenly; interest grows faster.

sections.heading: 6. Finding the instalment or the rate
sections.body_md:
- **Instalment:** write the interest as a multiple of $P$ (e.g. $n = 24$, $r = 9$: $I = 2.25P$), so $\text{MV} = 26.25P$; divide.
- **Rate:** first $I = \text{MV} - Pn$; then write $I$ as a multiple of $r$ (e.g. $P = 2000$, $n = 15$: $I = 200r$); divide.
- Answers often have paise or decimals (a rate of $6.5\%$); give them exactly.
- If an instalment must reach **at least** a target, round **up** to the next rupee.

sections.heading: 7. Finding the number of months
sections.body_md:
With $n$ unknown:

- **Interest given:** $n(n+1) = \dfrac{2400I}{Pr}$; find two consecutive whole numbers with this product.
- **Maturity value given:** $\text{MV} = Pn + \dfrac{Pr}{2400}\,n(n+1)$, a quadratic in $n$. Divide by the coefficient of $n^2$, factorise (or use the quadratic formula) and **reject the negative root**.

*Example:* ₹$1200$ a month at $8\%$ maturing to ₹18,960: $n^2 + 301n - 4740 = 0$, $(n - 15)(n + 316) = 0$, so $n = 15$.

Always check by working forwards.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Interest or maturity value (3 marks):* $n$ in months and the formula 1; substitution and interest 1; maturity value 1.
- *Instalment or rate (3–4 marks):* equation in $P$ or $r$ 1–2; solving 1; answer with units 1.
- *Number of months (4 marks):* equation 1; standard form 1; factorising 1; answer with the negative root rejected 1.
- *10-mark structured question:* parts (a), (b), (c) usually 3 + 3 + 4; show all working.

**Common mistakes**
1. Using years for $n$ (writing $n = 2$ for two years).
2. Forgetting to halve $n(n+1)$, or the $12$ in the denominator.
3. Simple interest on the whole deposit for the whole period.
4. Giving the interest when the maturity value is asked (or the reverse).
5. Finding the rate from the maturity value without first subtracting the deposits.
6. Keeping the negative root, or rounding an instalment down when a target must be reached.

questions.stem_md: Which description fits a recurring deposit account?

options.text_md: The depositor pays a fixed sum into the account every month for a chosen number of months.
The depositor pays one lump sum at the start and leaves it for a fixed period.
The depositor withdraws a fixed sum from the account every month.
The depositor pays a different sum each month, as and when convenient.

questions.solution_md: A recurring deposit collects equal monthly instalments for a fixed number of months; the bank pays the total with interest at maturity. Option (b) describes a fixed deposit.

questions.stem_md: In the recurring-deposit interest formula $I = P \times \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{r}{100}$, the letter $n$ stands for

options.text_md: the amount deposited each month
the number of monthly instalments
the number of years
the rate of interest per month

questions.solution_md: $n$ is the number of months (instalments); $P$ is the monthly instalment and $r$ the rate per cent per annum. A period in years must first be changed to months.

questions.stem_md: Shreya pays ₹600 a month into a recurring deposit for 10 months. The sum of her monthly balances, which is the principal for one month, is
questions.solution_md: Sum $= 600 \times \dfrac{10 \times 11}{2} = 600 \times 55 = 33000$. Option (d) is only the total deposited; (a) forgets to halve $n(n+1)$.

questions.stem_md: Interest earned on a recurring deposit of ₹400 a month for 12 months at 6% per annum is
questions.solution_md: $I = 400 \times \dfrac{12 \times 13}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{6}{100} = 156$. Option (a) charges interest on all ₹4,800 for the full year; (b) does not halve $n(n+1)$; (c) is the maturity value.

questions.stem_md: For a recurring deposit running for 2.5 years, the values to use for $n$ and $\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$ are
questions.solution_md: $2.5$ years $= 30$ months, so $n = 30$ and $\dfrac{30 \times 31}{2} = 465$. Option (c) forgets to halve.

questions.stem_md: Nandini deposits ₹900 every month for one year in a recurring deposit at 9% per annum. The amount she receives at maturity is
questions.solution_md: $I = 900 \times \dfrac{12 \times 13}{24} \times \dfrac{9}{100} = 526.50$; MV $= 10800 + 526.50$. Option (a) adds a full year's interest on the whole ₹10,800, which was not all in the bank for a year.

questions.stem_md: A 3-year recurring deposit of ₹700 a month matured to ₹28,308. The interest earned on it was
questions.solution_md: Total deposited $= 700 \times 36 = 25200$; interest $= 28308 - 25200 = 3108$. Option (a) adds instead of subtracting.

questions.stem_md: A recurring deposit of ₹1,000 a month for 2 years earns ₹2,250 as interest. The rate of interest per annum is
questions.solution_md: $2250 = 1000 \times \dfrac{24 \times 25}{24} \times \dfrac{r}{100} = 250r$, so $r = 9$. Option (a) uses $n(n+1)$ without halving.

questions.stem_md: The interest on a 12-month recurring deposit at 7% per annum is ₹1,365. The monthly instalment is
questions.solution_md: $1365 = P \times \dfrac{12 \times 13}{24} \times \dfrac{7}{100} = 0.455P$, so $P = 3000$. Option (b) treats ₹1,365 as a year's interest on one instalment.

questions.stem_md: A recurring deposit of ₹500 a month at 6% per annum has a maturity value of ₹6,195. Which equation gives the number of months n?
questions.solution_md: $6195 = 500n + 1.25n(n+1)$, so $1.25n^2 + 501.25n - 6195 = 0$; dividing by $1.25$ gives the equation in option (b). Option (d) leaves out the deposits $500n$.

questions.stem_md: While finding the period of a recurring deposit, Pranav reaches the equation $n^2 + n - 420 = 0$. The period is

options.text_md: 10 months
42 months
20 months
21 months

questions.solution_md: $n^2 + n - 420 = (n - 20)(n + 21) = 0$, so $n = 20$ or $n = -21$. A number of months cannot be negative, so the period is $20$ months.

questions.stem_md: Two recurring deposits have the same monthly instalment and the same rate; one runs for 12 months and the other for 24 months. The ratio of their interests is
questions.solution_md: The interest is proportional to $n(n+1)$: $\dfrac{12 \times 13}{24 \times 25} = \dfrac{156}{600} = \dfrac{13}{50}$. It is not $1 : 2$, because the longer deposit's early instalments stay much longer.

questions.stem_md: Under the ICSE method, the interest on a recurring deposit is worked out as

options.text_md: simple interest on each instalment for the number of months it stays in the account
compound interest on the total amount deposited
simple interest on the total amount deposited for the whole period
a fixed bonus added at maturity

questions.solution_md: The first instalment earns interest for n months, the second for n − 1 months, and so on; adding these simple interests gives the formula. Option (c) overstates the interest.

questions.stem_md: Devika pays ₹2,500 a month for 12 months into a recurring deposit at 8% per annum. Her maturity value is
questions.solution_md: $I = 2500 \times \dfrac{12 \times 13}{24} \times \dfrac{8}{100} = 1300$; MV $= 30000 + 1300$. Option (d) is a year's interest on all ₹30,000; (a) uses $n(n+1)$ without halving.

questions.stem_md: Plan X is a recurring deposit of ₹1,000 a month for 24 months at 6% per annum; Plan Y is one of ₹1,000 a month for 12 months at 12% per annum. Which statement about the interest is true?

options.text_md: Plan Y earns ₹720 more than Plan X.
Plan X earns exactly twice as much as Plan Y.
Plan X earns ₹720 more than Plan Y.
Both plans earn the same interest.

questions.solution_md: Plan X: $1000 \times \dfrac{24 \times 25}{24} \times \dfrac{6}{100} = 1500$. Plan Y: $1000 \times \dfrac{12 \times 13}{24} \times \dfrac{12}{100} = 780$. Difference $= 720$ in favour of X: doubling the period does more than doubling the rate.

questions.stem_md: If the monthly instalment of a recurring deposit is doubled, with the period and the rate unchanged, then the maturity value

options.text_md: becomes more than double
becomes less than double
does not change
is doubled

questions.solution_md: Both parts of MV $= Pn + P \times \dfrac{n(n+1)}{24} \times \dfrac{r}{100}$ are proportional to $P$, so MV doubles.

questions.stem_md: A recurring deposit of ₹500 a month at 6% per annum earned ₹340 as interest. For how many months did it run?
questions.solution_md: $340 = 500 \times \dfrac{n(n+1)}{24} \times \dfrac{6}{100}$ gives $n(n+1) = 272 = 16 \times 17$, so $n = 16$. Option (b) takes the larger factor.

questions.stem_md: In a 12-month recurring deposit of ₹1,200 a month at 9% per annum, how much interest does the first instalment alone earn?
questions.solution_md: The first instalment stays all $12$ months: $1200 \times \dfrac{12}{12} \times \dfrac{9}{100} = 108$. The last one earns only ₹9; ₹702 is the interest on all twelve.

questions.stem_md: The maturity value of a recurring deposit is

options.text_md: the last monthly instalment
the total of the instalments without any interest
the total of all the instalments together with the interest, paid at the end of the period
the interest earned on the deposit

questions.solution_md: MV = P × n + I: the bank returns every instalment and adds the interest when the period ends.

questions.stem_md: For a recurring deposit of ₹$P$ a month for $n$ months, the sum of the monthly balances (the principal for one month) is

options.text_md: $P \times n$
$P \times n(n+1)$
$P \times \dfrac{n+1}{2}$
$P \times \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$

questions.solution_md: The balances are $P, 2P, \ldots, nP$, and $1 + 2 + \cdots + n = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$. Option (a) is only the total deposited.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** For a recurring deposit of ₹300 a month for 10 months at 8% per annum, the interest is ₹110.

**Reason (R):** The ten monthly balances add up to ₹16,500, and this sum earns simple interest for one month.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: $16500 \times \dfrac{1}{12} \times \dfrac{8}{100} = 110$. Both are true and R is exactly how the formula is built.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The interest on a recurring deposit is simple interest, not compound interest.

**Reason (R):** The rate of interest on a recurring deposit is quoted per annum.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but quoting the rate per year does not explain why the interest is simple; that comes from the method (interest on each instalment for its own time, never on earlier interest).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** With the instalment and the rate fixed, a 24-month recurring deposit earns more than twice the interest of a 12-month one.

**Reason (R):** The interest on a recurring deposit is directly proportional to the number of months.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: The interest is proportional to $n(n+1)$, not to $n$: $\dfrac{24 \times 25}{12 \times 13} = \dfrac{600}{156} \approx 3.85$. A is true; R is false.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The maturity value of a recurring deposit of ₹$P$ a month for $n$ months at $r\%$ per annum is $P \times n \times \left(1 + \dfrac{r}{100}\right)$.

**Reason (R):** The maturity value is the total of the instalments plus the interest earned.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true. A is false: it gives a full year's interest on every rupee. For ₹1,000 a month for 24 months at 6%, A gives $25440$ but the correct MV is $24000 + 1500 = 25500$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The equation $n^2 + 241n - 8130 = 0$ comes from a recurring deposit of ₹800 a month at 10% per annum maturing to ₹27,100, so the deposit ran for 30 months.

**Reason (R):** The roots are $30$ and $-271$; a number of instalments must be a positive whole number, so $-271$ is rejected.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: $(n - 30)(n + 271) = 0$. R gives the reason for choosing $30$, so R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The last instalment of a 12-month recurring deposit earns interest for 12 months.

**Reason (R):** The first instalment of a recurring deposit earns interest for the whole period.

options.text_md: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true. The last instalment is paid in the final month and earns interest for only one month, so A is false.

questions.stem_md: In a recurring deposit account, the same amount is deposited every month.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: Equal monthly instalments are what make the deposit "recurring".

questions.stem_md: If the period of a recurring deposit is doubled, with the instalment and the rate unchanged, the interest is also exactly doubled.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: Interest depends on $n(n+1)$. For 12 and 24 months it goes from $78$ to $300$ units: almost four times.

questions.stem_md: When the rate is more than zero, the maturity value of a recurring deposit is always more than the total of the instalments.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: MV is the total of the instalments plus the interest, and the interest is positive when the rate is positive.

questions.stem_md: For a recurring deposit of 2 years, the value n = 2 is used in the interest formula.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: $n$ counts months: 2 years $= 24$ months, so $n = 24$.

questions.stem_md: When the number of months of a recurring deposit is found from a quadratic equation, both roots of the equation are possible periods.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: One root is always negative here, and a period must be a positive whole number of months, so only the positive root is kept.

questions.stem_md: In the recurring-deposit interest formula, r is the rate of interest per cent per month.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: $r$ is the rate per cent per annum; the factor $\dfrac{1}{12}$ in the formula turns the one-month principal into a fraction of a year.

questions.stem_md: For a recurring deposit of 24 months, the value of $\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$ is ___.
A recurring deposit running for one and a half years has n = ___ in the interest formula.
questions.solution_md: $1.5 \times 12 = 18$ months.

questions.stem_md: Maturity value of a recurring deposit = total of the monthly instalments + ___.
questions.solution_md: MV = P × n + I: the instalments come back with the interest.

questions.stem_md: At 5% per annum, Pranjal's recurring deposit of ₹1,500 a month for one year earns ₹___ in interest.
questions.solution_md: $I = 1500 \times \dfrac{12 \times 13}{24} \times \dfrac{5}{100} = 487.50$.

questions.stem_md: If the number of months $n$ of a recurring deposit satisfies $n(n+1) = 600$, then $n$ = ___.
questions.solution_md: $24 \times 25 = 600$, and the period must be positive, so $n = 24$.

questions.stem_md: In a 15-month recurring deposit, the 4th monthly instalment earns interest for ___ months.
questions.solution_md: It is in the account from month 4 to month 15: $15 - 4 + 1 = 12$ months.

questions.stem_md: Uma paid ₹800 monthly for 10 months into a recurring deposit and was credited ₹220 of interest. Her maturity value is ₹___.
Find the interest, in rupees, on a recurring deposit of ₹850 per month for 16 months at 9% per annum.
questions.solution_md: $I = 850 \times \dfrac{16 \times 17}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{9}{100} = 867$. The interest is ₹867.

questions.stem_md: Chitra puts ₹1,350 into a recurring deposit each month for 20 months; the bank pays 8% per annum. How many rupees does she receive at maturity?
questions.solution_md: $I = 1350 \times \dfrac{20 \times 21}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{8}{100} = 1890$; $\text{MV} = 1350 \times 20 + 1890 = 27000 + 1890 = 28890$. The maturity value is ₹28,890.

questions.stem_md: A recurring deposit for 12 months at 7.5% per annum has a maturity value of ₹17,482.50. Find the monthly instalment in rupees.
questions.solution_md:
Let the monthly instalment be ₹$P$. Then $I = P \times \dfrac{12 \times 13}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{7.5}{100} = 0.4875P$.

$\text{MV} = P \times 12 + 0.4875P = 12.4875P$.

So $12.4875P = 17482.50$, giving $P = \dfrac{17482.50}{12.4875} = 1400$.

The monthly instalment is ₹1,400.

questions.stem_md: Lalitha deposits ₹1,500 a month for 16 months and receives ₹25,020 at maturity. Find the rate of interest per cent per annum.
questions.solution_md:
Total deposited $= 1500 \times 16 = 24000$, so $I = 25020 - 24000 = 1020$.

$I = 1500 \times \dfrac{16 \times 17}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{r}{100} = 170r$.

So $170r = 1020$, giving $r = \dfrac{1020}{170} = 6$.

The rate is 6% per annum.

questions.stem_md: Salim's monthly payments of ₹2,500 into a recurring deposit at 6% per annum grew to ₹52,625 at maturity. Find the number of monthly instalments he paid.
questions.solution_md:
$\text{MV} = P \times n + P \times \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{r}{100}$, so $52625 = 2500n + 2500 \times \dfrac{n(n+1)}{24} \times \dfrac{6}{100}$.

$52625 = 2500n + 6.25n(n+1)$, that is $6.25n^2 + 2506.25n - 52625 = 0$.

Dividing by $6.25$: $n^2 + 401n - 8420 = 0$.

$(n - 20)(n + 421) = 0$, so $n = 20$ or $n = -421$. The number of months cannot be negative, so $n = 20$.

The deposit ran for 20 months.

questions.stem_md: A recurring deposit of ₹650 a month runs for 14 months. Find the sum of the monthly balances (the principal for one month) in rupees.
questions.solution_md: $650 \times \dfrac{14 \times 15}{2} = 650 \times 105 = 68250$. The principal for one month is ₹68,250.

questions.stem_md: Rakesh saves ₹2,200 every month for two and a half years in a recurring deposit paying 7% per annum. What does he receive at maturity, in rupees?
A 2-year recurring deposit at 8% per annum earns ₹2,880 as interest. Find the monthly instalment in rupees.
questions.solution_md:
$I = P \times \dfrac{24 \times 25}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{8}{100} = 2P$.

So $2P = 2880$, giving $P = \dfrac{2880}{2} = 1440$.

The monthly instalment is ₹1,440.

questions.stem_md: Write the value of $n$ and of $\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$ for a recurring deposit that runs for (a) 9 months (b) 3 years.
questions.solution_md: Always change years into months before using the formula.

questions.stem_md: Harsh pays ₹350 every month for 8 months into a recurring deposit at 9% per annum. Calculate the interest he earns.

answer.model_answer_md:
$I = 350 \times \dfrac{8 \times 9}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{9}{100} = 94.50$.

Harsh earns ₹94.50 as interest.

questions.solution_md: Substitute P, n and r into the recurring-deposit formula with n in months.

questions.stem_md: Find the maturity value of a recurring deposit of ₹640 a month for 15 months at 7.5% per annum.

answer.model_answer_md:
$I = 640 \times \dfrac{15 \times 16}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{7.5}{100} = 480$.

$\text{MV} = 640 \times 15 + 480 = 9600 + 480 = 10080$, so the maturity value is ₹10,080.

questions.solution_md: Find the interest first, then add the total of the instalments.

questions.stem_md: Kavya deposited ₹500 a month for one year and received ₹6,227.50 at maturity. Find the rate of interest.

answer.model_answer_md:
Total deposited $= 500 \times 12 = 6000$, so $I = 6227.50 - 6000 = 227.50$.

$I = 500 \times \dfrac{12 \times 13}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{r}{100} = 32.5r$.

So $32.5r = 227.50$, giving $r = \dfrac{227.50}{32.5} = 7$.

The rate of interest is 7% per annum.

questions.solution_md: Subtract the deposits from the maturity value to get the interest, then solve for r.

questions.stem_md: Joseph pays ₹250 a month into a recurring deposit for 5 months at 12% per annum. Make a table of his balance at the end of each month, find the sum of the balances, and hence find the interest.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Month | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Balance (₹) | 250 | 500 | 750 | 1000 | 1250 |

Sum of balances $= 250 + 500 + 750 + 1000 + 1250 = 3750$, which is the principal for one month.

$I = 3750 \times \dfrac{1}{12} \times \dfrac{12}{100} = 37.50$.

Check: $I = 250 \times \dfrac{5 \times 6}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{12}{100} = 37.50$. The interest is ₹37.50.

questions.solution_md: Each month the balance grows by one instalment; the balances together earn interest for one month.

questions.stem_md: Farhan opens a recurring deposit of ₹1,800 a month for 2 years at 6.5% per annum. Find (a) the interest he earns (b) the amount he receives at maturity.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $n = 24$. $I = 1800 \times \dfrac{24 \times 25}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{6.5}{100} = 2925$, so the interest is ₹2,925.

(b) $\text{MV} = 1800 \times 24 + 2925 = 43200 + 2925 = 46125$, so Farhan receives ₹46,125.

questions.solution_md: Change 2 years to 24 months; the maturity value is the deposits plus the interest.

questions.stem_md: Aditi's recurring deposit at 8% per annum ran for 27 months and paid her ₹17,712 at maturity. Find her monthly instalment.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let the monthly instalment be ₹$P$. Then $I = P \times \dfrac{27 \times 28}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{8}{100} = 2.52P$.

$\text{MV} = P \times 27 + 2.52P = 29.52P$.

So $29.52P = 17712$, giving $P = \dfrac{17712}{29.52} = 600$.

Her monthly instalment was ₹600.

questions.solution_md: Write both the deposits and the interest in terms of P, then divide.

questions.stem_md: Sameer's recurring deposit of ₹700 a month at 8% per annum earned ₹980 as interest. For how many months did he deposit?

answer.model_answer_md:
$980 = 700 \times \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{8}{100}$, so $n(n+1) = \dfrac{980 \times 2400}{700 \times 8} = 420$.

$n^2 + n - 420 = 0 \Rightarrow (n - 20)(n + 21) = 0$, so $n = 20$ (the root $-21$ is rejected).

Sameer deposited for 20 months.

questions.solution_md: Make n(n + 1) the subject, then factorise and keep the positive root.

marking_scheme.step: n = 20 with the negative root rejected

questions.stem_md: Rohan worked out the interest on a recurring deposit of ₹1,000 a month for 18 months at 8% per annum as $18000 \times \dfrac{8}{100} \times \dfrac{18}{12} = 2160$. Explain his mistake and find the correct interest.

answer.model_answer_md:
Rohan charged interest on all ₹18,000 for the whole 18 months. In fact only the first instalment stays for 18 months; the second stays 17 months, and the last only 1 month, so his answer is too large.

Correct: $I = 1000 \times \dfrac{18 \times 19}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{8}{100} = 1140$.

The correct interest is ₹1,140, which is ₹1,020 less than Rohan's figure.

questions.solution_md: Each instalment earns interest only for the months it is in the bank.

questions.stem_md: Ishita deposits ₹2,400 a month in a recurring deposit for 3 years at 7% per annum. Find (a) the total amount she deposits (b) the interest she earns (c) the maturity value.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $n = 36$; total deposited $= 2400 \times 36 = 86400$, i.e. ₹86,400.

(b) $I = 2400 \times \dfrac{36 \times 37}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{7}{100} = 9324$, so the interest is ₹9,324.

(c) MV $= 86400 + 9324 = 95724$, so Ishita receives ₹95,724.

questions.solution_md: Use n = 36 months throughout.

questions.stem_md: Gaurav wants ₹28,710 at the end of 18 months from a recurring deposit at 8% per annum. What should his monthly instalment be? Verify your answer.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let the monthly instalment be ₹$P$. Then $I = P \times \dfrac{18 \times 19}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{8}{100} = 1.14P$.

$\text{MV} = P \times 18 + 1.14P = 19.14P$.

So $19.14P = 28710$, giving $P = \dfrac{28710}{19.14} = 1500$.

Check: $I = 1500 \times \dfrac{18 \times 19}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{8}{100} = 1710$ and $\text{MV} = 1500 \times 18 + 1710 = 27000 + 1710 = 28710$ ✓.

His monthly instalment should be ₹1,500.

questions.solution_md: Express the maturity value as a multiple of P.

questions.stem_md: A recurring deposit of ₹1,250 a month for 2.5 years has a maturity value of ₹41,375. Find the rate of interest per annum.

answer.model_answer_md:
$2.5$ years $= 30$ months.

Total deposited $= 1250 \times 30 = 37500$, so $I = 41375 - 37500 = 3875$.

$I = 1250 \times \dfrac{30 \times 31}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{r}{100} = 484.375r$.

So $484.375r = 3875$, giving $r = \dfrac{3875}{484.375} = 8$.

The rate of interest is 8% per annum.

questions.solution_md: Find the interest by subtracting the deposits, then form a linear equation in r.

questions.stem_md: Bhavna pays ₹750 a month into a recurring deposit at 10% per annum and receives ₹12,850 at maturity. Find the number of months for which she paid.

answer.model_answer_md:
$\text{MV} = P \times n + P \times \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{r}{100}$, so $12850 = 750n + 750 \times \dfrac{n(n+1)}{24} \times \dfrac{10}{100}$.

$12850 = 750n + 3.125n(n+1)$, that is $3.125n^2 + 753.125n - 12850 = 0$.

Dividing by $3.125$: $n^2 + 241n - 4112 = 0$.

$(n - 16)(n + 257) = 0$, so $n = 16$ or $n = -257$. The number of months cannot be negative, so $n = 16$.

Bhavna paid for 16 months.

questions.solution_md: The unknown n appears in both the deposits and the interest, which gives a quadratic.

marking_scheme.step: n = 16 with the negative root rejected

questions.stem_md: Two sisters each save ₹24,000 in a recurring deposit at 7.5% per annum. Anjali pays ₹1,200 a month for 20 months; Rhea pays ₹1,000 a month for 24 months. Who receives more at maturity, and by how much?

answer.model_answer_md:
Anjali: $I = 1200 \times \dfrac{20 \times 21}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{7.5}{100} = 1575$; MV $= 24000 + 1575 = 25575$.

Rhea: $I = 1000 \times \dfrac{24 \times 25}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{7.5}{100} = 1875$; MV $= 24000 + 1875 = 25875$.

Rhea receives more, by $25875 - 25575 = 300$, i.e. ₹300: her smaller instalments stay in the bank longer on average.

questions.solution_md: Both deposit the same total, so only the interest differs.

questions.stem_md: Tara pays ₹2,000 a month for 6 months into a recurring deposit at 9% per annum. (a) For how many months does each instalment earn interest? (b) Find the interest on each instalment and add them. (c) Verify your total with the formula.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The 1st to 6th instalments earn interest for 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 months.

(b) Interest on one instalment for $m$ months $= 2000 \times \dfrac{m}{12} \times \dfrac{9}{100} = 15m$:

| Instalment | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th | 5th | 6th |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Months | 6 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 |
| Interest (₹) | 90 | 75 | 60 | 45 | 30 | 15 |

Total $= 90 + 75 + 60 + 45 + 30 + 15 = 315$.

(c) $I = 2000 \times \dfrac{6 \times 7}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{9}{100} = 315$ ✓. The interest is ₹315.

questions.solution_md: Add the simple interest on each instalment for its own number of months.

questions.stem_md:
Meera opens a recurring deposit of ₹1,100 a month for 2 years at 8% per annum in an imagined Konkan Sahakari Bank.

(a) Find the interest she earns.

(b) Find the maturity value.

(c) If she had kept the same deposit going for 3 years at the same rate, how much more interest would she have earned?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $n = 24$. $I = 1100 \times \dfrac{24 \times 25}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{8}{100} = 2200$. Interest ₹2,200.

(b) $\text{MV} = 1100 \times 24 + 2200 = 26400 + 2200 = 28600$. Maturity value ₹28,600.

(c) For 3 years, $n = 36$: $I = 1100 \times \dfrac{36 \times 37}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{8}{100} = 4884$.

Extra interest $= 4884 - 2200 = 2684$, i.e. ₹2,684 more. The period is only $1.5$ times as long, yet the interest is more than double.

questions.solution_md: Use n in months in every part; the extra interest is the difference of two interests.

questions.stem_md:
Answer each part.

(a) A recurring deposit for 20 months at 9% per annum has a maturity value of ₹8,630. Find the monthly instalment.

(b) Pooja pays ₹1,800 a month for 20 months and receives ₹38,047.50. Find the rate of interest.

(c) A recurring deposit of ₹900 a month at 8% per annum matures to ₹24,450. Find the number of months.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Let the monthly instalment be ₹$P$. Then $I = P \times \dfrac{20 \times 21}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{9}{100} = 1.575P$.

$\text{MV} = P \times 20 + 1.575P = 21.575P$.

So $21.575P = 8630$, giving $P = \dfrac{8630}{21.575} = 400$.

The monthly instalment is ₹400.

(b) Total deposited $= 1800 \times 20 = 36000$, so $I = 38047.50 - 36000 = 2047.50$.

$I = 1800 \times \dfrac{20 \times 21}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{r}{100} = 315r$.

So $315r = 2047.50$, giving $r = \dfrac{2047.50}{315} = 6.5$.

The rate is 6.5% per annum.

(c) $\text{MV} = P \times n + P \times \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{r}{100}$, so $24450 = 900n + 900 \times \dfrac{n(n+1)}{24} \times \dfrac{8}{100}$.

$24450 = 900n + 3n(n+1)$, that is $3n^2 + 903n - 24450 = 0$.

Dividing by $3$: $n^2 + 301n - 8150 = 0$.

$(n - 25)(n + 326) = 0$, so $n = 25$ or $n = -326$. The number of months cannot be negative, so $n = 25$.

The deposit ran for 25 months.

questions.solution_md: Instalment and rate give linear equations; the number of months gives a quadratic.

questions.stem_md:
Tenzin pays ₹1,500 a month for 8 months into a recurring deposit at 10% per annum.

(a) Make a table of his balance at the end of each month and find the principal for one month.

(b) Find the interest, and check it with the formula.

(c) Find the maturity value. Express the interest as a percentage of the total deposited, and explain why it is less than 10%.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a)

| Month | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Balance (₹) | 1500 | 3000 | 4500 | 6000 | 7500 | 9000 | 10500 | 12000 |

Principal for one month $= 1500 + 3000 + \cdots + 12000 = 1500 \times \dfrac{8 \times 9}{2} = 1500 \times 36 = 54000$.

(b) $I = 54000 \times \dfrac{1}{12} \times \dfrac{10}{100} = 450$. Check: $I = 1500 \times \dfrac{8 \times 9}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{10}{100} = 450$ ✓. Interest ₹450.

(c) $\text{MV} = 1500 \times 8 + 450 = 12000 + 450 = 12450$; maturity value ₹12,450.

Interest as a percentage of the deposits $= \dfrac{450}{12000} \times 100 = 3.75\%$. It is less than $10\%$ because $10\%$ is a yearly rate, the deposit lasts only 8 months, and most instalments stay in the bank for only part of that time.

questions.solution_md: The balances together earn interest for one month; compare the interest with the deposits for the percentage.

questions.stem_md:
Gurpreet needs at least ₹50,000 in 2 years for college fees. An imagined Narmada Co-operative Bank offers 8% per annum on recurring deposits.

(a) Show that every ₹1 of monthly instalment grows to ₹26 at maturity.

(b) Find the smallest whole number of rupees he should deposit each month.

(c) With this instalment, find the interest and the maturity value, and state how much more than ₹50,000 he receives.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $n = 24$. On an instalment of ₹1: $I = 1 \times \dfrac{24 \times 25}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{8}{100} = 2$, so MV $= 1 \times 24 + 2 = 26$.

(b) He needs $26P \ge 50000$, so $P \ge \dfrac{50000}{26} \approx 1923.08$. With ₹1,923 he would get $26 \times 1923 = 49998$, which is short, so the smallest whole-rupee instalment is ₹1,924.

(c) $I = 1924 \times \dfrac{24 \times 25}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{8}{100} = 3848$; $\text{MV} = 1924 \times 24 + 3848 = 46176 + 3848 = 50024$.

He receives ₹50,024, which is ₹24 more than ₹50,000.

questions.solution_md: For a fixed n and r the maturity value is a fixed multiple of P; round the instalment up, not to the nearest rupee.

questions.stem_md:
Two imagined banks offer recurring deposits. Bank A pays 7% per annum on a 3-year deposit; Bank B pays 8% per annum on a 30-month deposit. Zoya can pay ₹1,000 a month.

(a) Find her interest and maturity value with Bank A.

(b) Find her interest and maturity value with Bank B.

(c) Bank B wants its 30-month deposit of ₹1,000 a month to earn ₹3,875 in interest. What rate should it offer?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $n = 36$: $I = 1000 \times \dfrac{36 \times 37}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{7}{100} = 3885$; $\text{MV} = 1000 \times 36 + 3885 = 36000 + 3885 = 39885$. Interest ₹3,885, maturity value ₹39,885.

(b) $n = 30$: $I = 1000 \times \dfrac{30 \times 31}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{8}{100} = 3100$; $\text{MV} = 1000 \times 30 + 3100 = 30000 + 3100 = 33100$. Interest ₹3,100, maturity value ₹33,100. (Bank A pays more interest, at a lower rate, because the deposit is longer.)

(c) $I = 1000 \times \dfrac{30 \times 31}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{r}{100} = 387.5r$.

So $387.5r = 3875$, giving $r = \dfrac{3875}{387.5} = 10$.

Bank B should offer 10% per annum.

questions.solution_md: Compare interests, not rates: the period changes n(n + 1).

questions.stem_md:
Answer each part.

(a) A recurring deposit of ₹600 a month at 9% per annum earns ₹1,350 as interest. Find the number of months.

(b) Find the maturity value of the deposit in part (a).

(c) Arjun pays ₹1,200 a month into a recurring deposit at 5% per annum and receives ₹26,355. Find the number of months.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $1350 = 600 \times \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{9}{100}$, so $n(n+1) = \dfrac{1350 \times 2400}{600 \times 9} = 600$.

$n^2 + n - 600 = 0 \Rightarrow (n - 24)(n + 25) = 0$, so $n = 24$ (the root $-25$ is rejected).

The deposit ran for 24 months.

(b) $\text{MV} = 600 \times 24 + 1350 = 14400 + 1350 = 15750$; the maturity value is ₹15,750.

(c) $\text{MV} = P \times n + P \times \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{r}{100}$, so $26355 = 1200n + 1200 \times \dfrac{n(n+1)}{24} \times \dfrac{5}{100}$.

$26355 = 1200n + 2.5n(n+1)$, that is $2.5n^2 + 1202.5n - 26355 = 0$.

Dividing by $2.5$: $n^2 + 481n - 10542 = 0$.

$(n - 21)(n + 502) = 0$, so $n = 21$ or $n = -502$. The number of months cannot be negative, so $n = 21$.

Arjun paid for 21 months.

questions.solution_md: When only the interest is given, n(n + 1) is found directly; when the maturity value is given, the deposits Pn also appear.

marking_scheme.step: (c) n = 21 with the negative root rejected

questions.stem_md:
Members of one family use recurring deposits.

(a) Kabir pays ₹450 a month for 15 months at 9% per annum. Find his interest and maturity value.

(b) His brother's 2-year deposit at 7% per annum earned ₹2,016 as interest. Find the brother's monthly instalment.

(c) Their mother pays ₹1,500 a month for 2 years and receives ₹39,375. Find the rate of interest.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $I = 450 \times \dfrac{15 \times 16}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{9}{100} = 405$; $\text{MV} = 450 \times 15 + 405 = 6750 + 405 = 7155$. Interest ₹405, maturity value ₹7,155.

(b) $n = 24$. $I = P \times \dfrac{24 \times 25}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{7}{100} = 1.75P$.

So $1.75P = 2016$, giving $P = \dfrac{2016}{1.75} = 1152$.

The brother paid ₹1,152 a month.

(c) Total deposited $= 1500 \times 24 = 36000$, so $I = 39375 - 36000 = 3375$.

$I = 1500 \times \dfrac{24 \times 25}{2 \times 12} \times \dfrac{r}{100} = 375r$.

So $375r = 3375$, giving $r = \dfrac{3375}{375} = 9$.

The rate is 9% per annum.

questions.solution_md: Part (a) is direct; (b) and (c) are linear equations in P and in r.
